us-policy-positions:agriculture-natural-.source: National Agricultural Law Center (Richardson), Water Rights Tables, October 31, 2016, Tables 1 and 2, read 9/29/2026 for the 50 states; New York's permit program page for its 2011 change; the Illinois Water Use Act of 1983; the Puerto Rico Water Law and Guam's water regulations for those territories.
us-policy-positions:agriculture-natural-.note: Yes: a state permit sets how much a large well may pump, across the whole state, and the amounts are reported or metered. No: the state only registers wells or collects reports, or limits pumping only in named areas or through local districts. Places whose law could not be read take the most common answer among similar places, marked ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE.

US-AK.note: Groundwater belongs to the first in time with a state permit, which sets how much each well may pump (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016: prior appropriation for groundwater).

US-AL.note: The state registers and collects reports of withdrawals above 100,000 gallons a day but sets no limit (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-AR.note: The state registers withdrawals but sets no limit (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-AS.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 2 territories read for this question (both answer yes), because this place's own law could not be read.
US-AS.note: Tried: the American Samoa Code Annotated at asbar.org, which refuses this container (HTTP 403), 9/29/2026.

US-AZ.note: The state limits groundwater only inside its Active Management Areas, not across the state (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-CA.note: The state has no state groundwater permit; local sustainability agencies manage basins under the 2014 Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-CO.note: Groundwater belongs to the first in time with a state permit, which sets how much each well may pump (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016: prior appropriation for groundwater).

US-CT.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 50,000 gallons a day (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-DC.estimated: ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE: the most common answer among the 50 states read for this question (31 answer yes), because the District's own rule could not be read; the District draws no groundwater (US Geological Survey, 2015), so the answer moves nothing.
US-DC.note: Not read on 9/29/2026: the District draws no groundwater (US Geological Survey, 2015), so its well rules were left for later.

US-DE.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 50,000 gallons a day (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-FL.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit from one of its five water management districts (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-GA.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 100,000 gallons a day (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-GU.note: The Water Resources Development and Operating Regulations require a well permit with a production meter, and cap each well's capacity at the pumping rates the Northern Lens Study sets for its management zone.

US-HI.note: The state requires water use permits only inside designated water management areas (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-IA.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 25,000 gallons a day (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-ID.note: Groundwater belongs to the first in time with a state permit, which sets how much each well may pump (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016: prior appropriation for groundwater).

US-IL.note: A new high-capacity well (100,000 gallons a day or more) must be reported to the soil and water conservation district, which reviews its effect on other users; the Water Use Act of 1983 requires no permit and sets no limit. The National Agricultural Law Center's 2016 table lists a permit here; the statute does not.

US-IN.note: The state registers and collects reports of withdrawals above 100,000 gallons a day but sets no limit (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-KS.note: Groundwater belongs to the first in time with a state permit, which sets how much each well may pump (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016: prior appropriation for groundwater).

US-KY.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 10,000 gallons a day, farms and homes exempt (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-LA.note: The state registers wells and collects reports above 1,000,000 gallons a day but sets no limit (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-MA.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 100,000 gallons a day (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-MD.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit for any withdrawal, small farms and homes exempt (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-ME.note: The state permits only select groundwater withdrawals and otherwise collects reports (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-MI.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 2,000,000 gallons a day and reports above 100,000 (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-MN.note: Large groundwater withdrawals need a permit above 10,000 gallons in a day or 1,000,000 in a year (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-MO.note: The state registers and collects reports of withdrawals above 100,000 gallons a day but sets no limit (National Agricultural Law Center, Water Rights Tables, 2016).

US-PR.note: The Water Law requires a permit to drill a well and a franchise to extract groundwater, and charges by the gallon extracted (farms exempt from the charge).
